summary: One seat decides who runs the body: {the body} is split down the middle, and {wavering member} is weighing a move that would hand control to the other side.
realLife: One life: With the Senate split 50-50 in January 2001, the outgoing vice president's tie-breaking vote made him majority leader for 17 days. In June a Vermont Republican left his caucus to become an independent, and control came back to Daschle. Another: When control flipped in June 2001 he became chair of the government affairs committee and pushed to fold border, emergency and coast agencies into one new department. Another: After he switched parties in 2009, his new colleagues refused to let him keep nearly 30 years of committee seniority.
gates: You hold a seat in {the body} or lead a party in it.
The seats are split so that one member changes who holds the majority.
weights: How far {wavering member}'s views sit from their party's.
choices: promise help in their next race
ask your own wavering members what they need first

branches.then: Your party runs the body, and the chairs change hands in the middle of the session.
